# Compound interest

## Pretest

<!-- tal:pretest -->
1. Someone invests 200 at five percent per year and leaves the interest in the account; how much do they hold two years later?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

220.50

</details>

2. Interest of half a percent is added to a loan each month; is the borrower's effective yearly cost above or below six percent?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

Above, because each month's charge is itself charged later.

</details>
<!-- /tal:pretest -->

## Interest on interest

A savings account can pay interest in two ways (slide 1, 0:42). Under simple interest the payment each period is fixed, because the bank only looks at the original deposit. Under compound interest the bank adds each payment to the balance, so later payments are computed on a larger base.

> With compound interest, the interest you earned is added to the balance, and next period it earns interest too. (slide 1, 1:15)

The lecturer sums this up as interest on interest. The difference from simple growth is small at first and gets larger with every period that passes.

How often the bank adds interest matters (slide 2, 2:40). Adding it more often means each payment starts earning sooner, so the effective annual rate ends up above the quoted APR. When two accounts quote rates on different schedules, convert both to effective annual rates before comparing them (slide 9).

<!-- tal:check -->
1. Which number should you use to rank savings accounts whose rates are quoted on different schedules?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

The effective annual rate of each account.

</details>
<!-- /tal:check -->
